hints: Which cells change? Only those you can reach from (row, col) by walking through cells of the same starting colour. Also: what happens if the new colour equals the old one?
A flood fill with DFS (an explicit stack avoids deep recursion). Remember the original colour; recolour a cell as you push it so it is never visited twice.

1. Let old = image[row][col]; if old == color, return the image unchanged.
  2. Recolour the start cell and push it.
  3. Pop a cell; for each of its 4 neighbours with colour old, recolour and push.
  4. Return the image when the stack is empty.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: DFS/BFS from the start cell over same-coloured neighbours; each cell is touched at most once.

explain: In [[1,1,0],[1,0,0],[1,1,1]] starting at (0,0) with colour 5, the old colour is 1. The fill spreads to (0,1), (1,0), (2,0), (2,1), (2,2) — all the 1s connected to the start — and leaves the 0s alone. Recolouring works as the 'visited' mark. The early return when old == color matters: without it the loop would keep finding 'old-coloured' cells forever.
recognize: Change a connected region of same-valued cells starting from one cell → flood fill with DFS/BFS.
